I use power to weight ratio to judge a car's potential, but it's only potential. There are so many variables in play. Gearing, transmission type, how power is made, power curve, tires, it goes on endlessly.

Just as a rule of thumb think of it this way. Most factory vehicles, just ordinary cars, fall somewhere around 20-23:1 power to weight ratio. That's 20-23 pounds per horsepower. That's kind of the mundane belt. But there are other factors, like torque and gearing.

Generally a manual transmission is better than a traditional automatic and a traditional automatic is better than a CVT. Also some vehicles, like diesels and especially turbo diesels make little power but a lot of torque. A certain diesel hatchback is as fast as a certain sportier version from 0-45ish, than falls off because it doesn't have the horsepower numbers to keep up.

Then there is the actual weight to consider. A 6000 pound vehicle with a 10:1 power to weight ratio will accelerate very quickly, but it's still a 3 ton car and may struggle in the corners and under braking. Whereas a 2300 pound car with a 17:1 ratio won't accelerate all that quickly, but is leaps and bounds better at braking and cornering. This is one of the reasons certain lightweight roadsters and certain older compact sedans are so popular.

Last is how power is made. So take a baseline 300HP. Look at a certain older muscle car, a certain all-wheel-drive performance sedan and let's say an older luxury grand tourer. That's a naturally aspirated V8, a turbo charged H4 and a supercharged I6. The NA-V8 will be very responsive and have a very natural torque curve making for good acceleration. The Turbo will take longer to spool up and build power (less true with newer and newer vehicles) and suffer the risk of losing boost with speed changes. The supercharger will be more similar to the NA-V8 with a linear torque curve but loses some initial power to parasitic loss.

All this info is great to have and learn more about but in the end the only reliable test of whether a car does what you want it to do is to drive it and see. The only benchmark is the seat of your pants.
